key_insight: A systematic empirical comparison shows that a few practical design choices—multimodal alignment between vision, language and actions, the breadth and quality of training data, and how actions are grounded—drive whether vision–language–action models become useful for generalist robots.
problem_solved: Clarifies which components and engineering trade-offs actually matter when building and evaluating vision–language–action models for embodied robotic tasks.
method: Empirical comparison of existing vision–language–action model families across a diverse set of embodied tasks.
Controlled ablation studies to isolate the effect of factors such as data scale/quality, multimodal alignment, architecture choices, and action grounding.
Evaluation using both simulated and real-world robotic tasks to measure task success, generalization, and instruction-following robustness.
impact: Gives practitioners an evidence-based roadmap for prioritizing data collection, model design and evaluation when developing generalist robot systems—reducing wasted effort on low-impact changes and accelerating practical deployment.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: perception → language understanding → action policy, with callouts showing where alignment and grounding choices apply.
Bar/importance chart: relative impact of factors (data, alignment, architecture, grounding) on downstream task performance.
Ablation heatmap: model variants × tasks showing performance drops when each component is removed or modified.
Photo/illustration montage: simulated vs. real-world robot tasks to highlight evaluation diversity.
paper_title: What matters in building vision–language–action models for generalist robots
paper_authors: Xinghang Li, Peiyan Li, Long Qian, Minghuan Liu, Dong Wang
